acts.title: The ring in the garden
text: I heard this from a friend, and I still don’t quite believe it.

In 1995 my friend’s mother was baking in her kitchen when she noticed that her wedding ring had gone. She had been wearing it that morning — she was sure of that. She searched the flour, the bin and the sink. In the end her husband took up part of the kitchen floor. They found two coins, a button and a great deal of dust, but no ring.
For the next ten years nobody mentioned it. She wore a cheap silver one instead and said she had stopped thinking about it, which was not true.

Then, one afternoon in 2005, she was digging up carrots at the end of the garden. She pulled one out, turned it over and stopped. The carrot had grown straight through the ring. It had been lying in the soil the whole time, and the vegetable had simply come up around it.
By the time she got back to the house she was laughing so much that nobody could understand her. She wears it again now. As far as I know, she has never taken it off since.

items.r: makes the listener want to hear it
sets the scene and says what went wrong
covers the years in between quickly
gives the surprise the story was built for
closes the story and brings it up to now

acts.title: The phrases that hold it together
text: My friend’s mother was baking in her kitchen when she noticed that her ring had gone.
She had been wearing it that morning.
In the end her husband took up part of the kitchen floor.
Then, one afternoon in 2005, she was digging up carrots.
By the time she got back to the house she was laughing.
As far as I know, she has never taken it off since.

acts.genre: Register · told aloud or written down
acts.title: Spoken story or written narrative?
text: A story told aloud is full of short reactions, questions back to the listener and unfinished sentences. The listener does half the work.
A written narrative has no listener to react, so it does the work itself: full sentences, paragraphs, and linkers that make the order clear.

And then — you’ll love this — she looked at the carrot.
For the next ten years nobody mentioned it.

lines: She [was baking|baked|had baked] when she [noticed|was noticing|had noticed] that the ring had gone.
She [had been wearing|was wearing once|has worn] it that morning, so she knew it was in the flat.
[By the time|As soon as|While] her husband finished with the floor, they [had found|found already|have found] two coins and a button.
Ten years later she [was digging|dug once|had dug] up carrots [when|until|by the time] she saw it.
She [has worn|wore|had worn] it every day since then.

items.why: last Tuesday is finished time, so the past simple is used.
remind here describes a state, so the simple form is used.
A story about the future of your memory takes will: I’ll never forget that day.

write.q: Write your own narrative of about 200 words, following the model: an opening line that makes the reader want to go on, the scene and the problem, the years or hours in between, the surprise, and a closing line that brings it up to now.
write.model:
You’ll never believe what happened to my grandfather in 1978.

He was travelling home from Almaty by train when he realized that his suitcase had gone. He had put it under the seat at the start of the journey. He searched the whole carriage, and a guard searched the next one, but by the time they reached the station it was clear that somebody had taken it.

For eleven years he told the story at every family dinner, always in the same words.

Then, in 1989, a woman phoned. She had bought a flat in Karaganda, and while she was clearing out the cupboard she had found an old suitcase with his name and address inside it. Nothing was missing except a bar of chocolate.

He kept that suitcase until he died. It is in my mother’s flat now, and she has never let anybody throw it away.

speak.q: Tell your story out loud to an imaginary listener. Pause where the listener would react, and use “So then…” to move it forward.
